thread.title: Markets Now: Dow Gains 30 Points as Apple Beats, Fed Clock Ticks - Barron's

author: Ben Levisohn
title: Markets Now: Dow Gains 30 Points as Apple Beats, Fed Clock Ticks - Barron's
text:
By Ben Levisohn Updated May 2, 2018 2:32 p.m. ET Want to know why the Dow Jones Industrial Average is doing what it's doing? Check back here for a semi-live look at the volatile markets from Barron's reporters.
Illustration: Bloomberg News 2:27 p.m. I've been doing this long enough to know that there are always three reactions to a Fed meeting: the initial one, the reversal of the first one, and the right one. We've had the first two, as the market popped, and then gave back all its post Fed gains.
Now it's trying to figure out what the right one is. The D ow Jones Industrial Average is up 14.68 points, or 0.1%, at 24,113.73, while the S&P 500 is little changed at 2654.58 and the Nasdaq Composite has risen 0.3%, to 7151.95.
What's amusing about all this is that nothing really has changed. "Bottom line, the rise in inflation to basically 2% is what the Fed has been hoping for and forecasting and therefore they don’t yet feel the need to alter the pace of their tightening path," writes Bleakley Advisory Group's Peter Boockvar .
Did anyone expect anything different?
Dow Gains 80 Points as Fed Shocks No One
2:10 p.m. It's the moment we've all been waiting for— the Federal Open Market Committee statement is live . And the market appears to like it, though it may not be obvious from looking at where the indexes are now. The S&P 500 has ticked up 0.2% to 2659.198, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average has advanced 80.66 points, or 0.3%, to 24,179.71. The Nasdaq Composite has risen 0.5% to 7,165.18.
But the actual gains came following the announcements, as this chart shows:
Why the "rejoicing," if a 0.1% rise can be called that? The Fed kept rates unchanged, no surprise there, and said inflation had "moved close" to its 2% target. But it didn't say anything that shocked the market either: It called the economic risks "roughly balanced;" dropped a sentence about economic activity strengthening, and repeated that the economy needed more hikes in the future. "There is very little new in the FOMC statement," writes Seaport Global's Tom Digaloma .
And that's music to the market's ears.
Dow Drops 50 Points as Fed Clock Keeps Ticking
12:21 p.m. The market really has gone nowhere today, and why should it with the Fed on deck? The Dow Jones Industrial Average is down 51.96 points, or 0.2%, at 24,047.09, while the S&P 500 has declined 0.3% to 2647.62 and the Nasdaq Composite is off 0.1% to 7123.71.
There is no press conference or public event around today's meeting, so it could be uneventful. But then again, maybe not. "Look for words that cite the inflation pickup and continued growth in the economy," writes NatAlliance Securities' Andrew Brenner . "This should send rates higher, probably breaking the recent 3.03%."
And won't the market just love that?
Dow Gains 30 Points as Apple Beats, Fed Clock Ticks
6:48 a.m. It's Fed day, and boy, is the market...not doing much yet. S&P 500 futures have ticked up 0.1%, while Dow Jones Industrial Average futures have advanced 29 points, or 0.1%, and Nasdaq Composite futures have risen 0.3%.
While all the focus is on the Federal Reserve—don't expect much from today's meeting—we shouldn't forget that we're still in the heart of earnings season. Apple (AAPL) has gained 3.3% to $174.93 in pre-open trading after its beat , and it's not the only company to be topping estimates. Credit Suisse strategist Jonathan Golub notes that earnings have risen at an 18% clip excluding tax benefits, and companies have been beating by 8%.
Of course, the market hasn't been responding to the outstanding results, but Golub insists they should be. "Concerns surrounding peaking EPS and economic growth, rising inflation/rates, a flattening yield curve , and a maturing business cycle are weighing on stocks," Golub writes. "While each issue has merit, we believe investors are under-estimating the market's potential upside, and over-estimating risks."
Unless, of course, they're not.
